doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: The student who did not know Tiny Kahn, and Billy Cobham
summary: Anecdotes of students lacking curiosity, including one who never explored Billy Cobham, and Soph's warning about commitment.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Drummer magazine?” He said, “Yeah, I do.” I said, “Did you see that article about Tiny Kahn?” And I said, “Great article” by I think Burt Korall had written it. And the kid goes, “Yeah I saw it.” I said, “Did you read it?” He said, “No. I didn’t read it.” I said, “Why didn’t you read it?” Are you ready for this? His answer was, “Because I didn’t know who he is.”
There’s a weird loop to that thing.

Yeah. And I just said to this young man, I said, do you realize what you just said? Do you wear the same clothes every day? Do you have the same conversations every day? I mean damn. And the other trick that I would use with them is I put on, I had a deal with my students. They’d give me the stuff they’re listening to, all the current stuff, and I hip them to the stuff that I grew up with when I was their age. So I put on Mahavishnu “Inner Mounting Flame.” Billy Cobham. And this kid goes, “God, who is that?” And I said, “That’s Billy Cobham, and he’s doing that on a four-piece drum set.” “You’ve got to be kidding.”

Something like that, yeah. And I said, “Are you familiar with Billy Cobham?” And of the course the classic answer: “I know his name.” “Okay” I said, “now you’ve got his music, are you excited about this?” “My God” he says, “I can’t believe it, I can’t believe it. I’m going to go check him out.” Okay. So I wait maybe three weeks, three more lessons go by. The student comes in I said, “Okay, I’m ready for it.” He goes, “What’s that?” “Tell me what you found.” And he said, “Found, what do you mean?” “Well Billy Cobham, you said you were going to dig deep into Billy Cobham.” “Oh man, I had an English exam” and blah-blah-blah. And I say now those are the kind of people, I tell them I say, “If that’s how you pursue things that really turn you on” — meaning you don’t pursue them at all — you have no business going into music. Absolutely no business at all. You can do it for fun, become a stockbroker, a doctor, a lawyer, a dentist, anything. But you’re not going to make it if you don’t have — because the people who are your competition, to put it in capitalistic terms, they’re good because they welcome what they don’t know and when then discover what they don’t know they go for it. And if you don’t do that you don’t have a snowball’s chance in hell.
I’ve been saying it a long time.
